name: Face slimming strap
lead: A face slimming strap is an elastic band worn under the chin and over the head or ears to compress the lower face and neck. It is marketed for reducing the look of a double chin and defining the jawline and is sold mainly through online marketplaces and social media. Similar straps, called chin straps, are also used in medical settings, for example to keep the mouth closed during positive airway pressure therapy.[1]

No published clinical study appears to have tested compression straps for slimming the face or reducing submental fat. Published reviews of non-surgical treatments for submental fullness cover injectable deoxycholic acid, cryolipolysis, radiofrequency, focused ultrasound and similar interventions, and do not mention compression straps.[2][3] A small case report of a commercially sold jaw exerciser reported no change in jawline or double chin.[4]
Proponents say that compression briefly pushes fluid away or holds the jaw in a tighter position; there is no evidence that the effect persists once the strap is removed.

paras: Face slimming straps are typically made of stretchy fabric with a hook-and-loop or adjustable closure. Some versions are described as V-line or sleep straps and are marketed to be worn for hours or overnight. The strap sits under the chin and over the crown or in front of the ears, applying upward pressure.

The claimed mechanism is external compression of the submental region, which proponents say may temporarily shift fluid or hold the soft tissue in a more defined position. Fat reduction in the neck by established methods works by destroying fat cells chemically or with energy delivered to the tissue, as described in reviews of deoxycholic acid injection and cryolipolysis.[2] A compression band does not use these mechanisms.
No studies found of compression straps for slimming the face or reducing a double chin.

A 2026 systematic review of 30 studies of nonsurgical treatments for submental fullness covered injectable deoxycholic acid (17 studies), cryolipolysis (11), radiofrequency (3), novel injectables, focused ultrasound, diode laser and a combined device, with liposuction for comparison. A pooled analysis of eight deoxycholic acid studies found a responder proportion of 70.8 percent with high heterogeneity, and adverse events were mostly mild and transient. The review did not include compression garments or straps, and its authors noted that many included studies were open-label or industry-sponsored.[2]
Deoxycholic acid injection (ATX-101) was approved for submental fat in the United States as Kybella and in Canada as Belkyra, and trials reported common injection-site reactions.[5]

A 2024 case report followed two men who used a commercially available silicone jaw exerciser for about three months, one to three times a week. Neither participant showed a change in double chin, jawline or face and neck tightness by before-and-after photographs, and neither was satisfied with the product's feel. Both participants were also authors, no objective measurements were taken, and the authors called for larger studies.[4]

Reported or plausible issues include skin irritation, pressure marks and discomfort, and the possibility that a tight strap interferes with comfortable breathing or sleep. No safety study of cosmetic straps has been published. Medical chin straps used with positive airway pressure have been studied for their effect on treatment compliance, which is a separate application.[1]

Straps are discussed alongside jaw exercisers and mewing-related devices as inexpensive options for jawline definition. Advocates say that the visual tightening is noticeable while the strap is worn. No published study has measured sustained change.

timeline.event: Phase III trial reports on patient experience with ATX-101 (Kybella/Belkyra), approved for submental fat.[5]
Case report of two men using a commercial jaw exerciser finds no change in double chin or jawline.[4]
